explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. She says, "Do not spend your strength on women or your vigor on those who ruin kings." (Proverbs 31:3) So the warning is about where a king pours his vigor, and she names the ones who ruin kings. Lemuel's mother is not mincing words here, and I respect it.

Flattery sounds like a very kingly problem, I'll give you that. But the text says "those who ruin kings." (Proverbs 31:3) Nothing about flattery shows up in her warning. Her words are short and they hit hard.

Serving a king sounds harmless, like a nice helper with a tray of cookies. But her line says "those who ruin kings." (Proverbs 31:3) That's the group she warns him about, and serving isn't in it. Her warning is about where his vigor goes.

That's it, baker. She tells Lemuel, "It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine…" (Proverbs 31:4) She says it twice, so she means it. When Mama repeats herself, you don't ask for a third round.

War feels like a big kingly topic, so I see why you went there. But her line is about something else: "it is not for kings to drink wine…" (Proverbs 31:4) War never comes up in these verses. She keeps it close to home.

Palaces would be a fun thing to bring up with a king! But she says, "it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to crave strong drink." (Proverbs 31:4) No palaces anywhere in her talk. Just wine and strong drink.

Right on the money. She says it's "lest they drink and forget what is decreed…" (Proverbs 31:5) A ruler is supposed to remember what is decreed. I can't even keep track of my own oven timer on a good day, so a king with a whole kingdom has a lot to remember.
That would be a rough day for a king, no doubt. But her words are "lest they drink and forget what is decreed…" (Proverbs 31:5) She never mentions an army. The trouble she names is forgetting.

explanations.answer: They bring shame on the palace
explanations.explanation: Shame on the palace sounds like something a mother would worry about, I get it. But the text doesn't say that. It says "lest they drink and forget what is decreed…" (Proverbs 31:5) Forgetting is the danger she names.

Yes, friend. The ruler who forgets ends up "depriving all the oppressed of justice." (Proverbs 31:5) The oppressed are the ones who pay when a ruler forgets. I think that's why she wants Lemuel's head clear.
I can see why you'd guess the wealthy. But the verse says "depriving all the oppressed of justice." (Proverbs 31:5) The wealthy aren't named there. The oppressed are the ones left without justice.

Priests are a fair guess, since they show up in plenty of Bible places. Not here, though. The text says "depriving all the oppressed of justice." (Proverbs 31:5) The oppressed are the people in her sights.

That's the one. She says, "Let him drink and forget his poverty…" (Proverbs 31:7) Her words are for the one who is perishing and the one who is bitter in soul. Notice who she's looking at: someone hurting, not a king on his throne.

Enemies make a good guess, but they never show up in her words. She says, "Let him drink and forget his poverty…" (Proverbs 31:7) The thing he forgets is his poverty. Her words stay on his hard situation.
I get why sins came to mind, since that's a weighty topic. But the verse says, "Let him drink and forget his poverty…" (Proverbs 31:7) Sins aren't in it. Poverty is what she names.

Nailed it, baker. She says, "Open your mouth for those with no voice…" (Proverbs 31:8) A king has a voice that carries, so she tells him to use it for people who don't have one. That's a mighty big job for a mouth.

Wisdom is a very Proverbs kind of word, so I see the pull. But her line says, "Open your mouth for those with no voice…" (Proverbs 31:8) The king's mouth is for people who have no voice. That's the whole point of the line.

Faith is a good word, and it just isn't the one in this line. She says, "Open your mouth for those with no voice…" (Proverbs 31:8) The people she names are those with no voice. Their voice is what's missing, so the king speaks up.

True, friend. She says, "Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed." (Proverbs 31:8) The dispossessed are right there in the verse. She's got a long list of people for the king to speak up for.

It's actually true. The verse says, "Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed." (Proverbs 31:8) The dispossessed are named right there. Lemuel's mother tells him to open his mouth for them too.

Yes, baker. She says, "Open your mouth, judge righteously, and defend the cause of the poor and needy." (Proverbs 31:9) Speaking up and judging righteously go together in her words. A king who judges righteously is one who also remembers the poor.

Ruling with power sounds like a regular king job, I know. But her line says, "Open your mouth, judge righteously, and defend the cause of the poor and needy." (Proverbs 31:9) Power isn't what she asks for. She asks him to judge righteously.

Guarding the throne is what I'd expect a king to hear. Her words go a different way: "Open your mouth, judge righteously, and defend the cause of the poor and needy." (Proverbs 31:9) Nothing about a throne. She wants him to judge righteously.

That one's a trap, friend, and I almost stepped in it myself. Her last line says, "defend the cause of the poor and needy." (Proverbs 31:9) The rich aren't named in it. She points the king toward the poor and needy.

Right, it's false. Her words are, "Open your mouth, judge righteously, and defend the cause of the poor and needy." (Proverbs 31:9) The rich aren't in that line. She tells the king to defend the cause of the poor and needy.
